slides: In the first lesson we counted in stages. Now let's see what happens when a stage has a restriction.

slides.say: Restrictions are what make counting questions hard. So we'll go slowly, with three kinds of restriction.
The first restriction is a number can't start with zero. Let's count all the two-digit numbers.
Two stages, the tens digit and the units digit.
Can the tens digit be zero? No. There is no number zero seven. We just write seven, and that's a one-digit number.
at: There is no number zero seven

slides.say: So the tens digit is one to nine. That's nine options.
The units digit has no restriction. It can be anything from zero to nine. That's ten options.
Nine times ten is ninety. So there are ninety two-digit numbers.
Let's check it another way. The two-digit numbers go from ten to ninety-nine. Ninety-nine minus ten, plus one, is ninety. The same answer.
Now a new example. How many three-digit numbers are even?
at: How many three-digit numbers are even

slides.say: Three stages, the hundreds, the tens and the units.

slides: Which stage has the restriction? An even number ends in an even digit. So the units digit is the one with the restriction. We start with it.

slides.say: The units digit can be zero, two, four, six or eight. That's five options.
The hundreds digit can't be zero, so one to nine. Nine options.
And the tens digit is free. Ten options.
Nine times ten is ninety. Then ninety times five is four hundred fifty.
A check. There are nine hundred three-digit numbers, from a hundred to nine hundred ninety-nine. Half of them are even, and half of nine hundred is four hundred fifty.
at: There are nine hundred three-digit numbers

slides: So always start with the stage that has the restriction. The free stages can wait, because they work with anything.

slides.say: The third restriction is the hardest one. Sometimes one choice decides another choice.
Let's see it. How many two-digit numbers have a digit sum of eleven? That means the two digits add up to eleven.
at: How many two-digit numbers have a digit sum

slides.say: We start with the first digit. Can it be zero? Then the second digit would need to be eleven. But eleven is a number, not a digit.
Can it be one? Then the second digit would need to be ten, and ten isn't a digit either.
Two works, because two plus nine is eleven. So the first digit is two to nine. That's eight options.
at: So the first digit is two to nine

slides.say: Now the second digit. Imagine we already picked the first digit, say six. What completes six to eleven? Only five.
And if we picked nine? Only two completes it. Whatever we pick first, exactly one digit completes it.
So the second stage is forced. It has one option. Eight times one is eight.
Let's list them to see it. Twenty-nine, thirty-eight, forty-seven, and so on up to ninety-two. Eight numbers.
Careful here. A lot of students give the second digit ten options, or eight. But the second digit isn't free. It depends on the first one, so it gets one.
One more example. How many two-digit numbers have a units digit that is twice the tens digit?
at: How many two-digit numbers have a units digit

slides.say: The tens digit first. It can't be zero. Can it be five? Two times five is ten, and ten isn't a digit.
So the tens digit is one, two, three or four. Four options.
at: So the tens digit is one

slides.say: Once we pick the tens digit, the units digit is forced. It must be twice the tens digit. One option.
Four times one is four. And here they are, twelve, twenty-four, thirty-six and forty-eight.
So let's sum it up. A number never starts with zero.
at: A number never starts with zero

slides.say: Start with the stage that has the restriction.
And if one choice decides another, imagine you already picked the first one. Then ask what completes it. The forced stage gets one.
Take a moment to memorize this, and I'll see you in the next video.
